summary: This Standards Track document describes DMARC failure reports, which give details about individual messages that failed to authenticate under DMARC. It updates RFC 6591 and obsoletes RFC 7489.

eli5.summary: When a letter fails the fake check, the post office sends the school a note about that one letter.

questions: what is a dmarc failure report
what is the ruf tag in dmarc
subtitle: Per-message DMARC failure reports that tell a domain owner exactly which mail failed authentication, and the privacy cost of sending them.

tldr.problem: Aggregate DMARC reports give totals but not the details of a particular failed message, which makes it hard to find the cause of a failure or spot direct abuse of a domain quickly.
tldr.mechanism: A Mail Receiver sends a failure report in the RFC 6591 abuse report format shortly after a DMARC failure, to the addresses in the ruf tag. RFC 9991 adds an Identity-Alignment field and a dmarc Auth-Failure type.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9991 updates RFC 6591 and, with RFC 9989 and RFC 9990, obsoletes RFC 7489. It warns that reports can expose personal data, and many large providers limit or disable them.

today: RFC 9991 is a Proposed Standard from May 2026. It updates RFC 6591 and obsoletes RFC 7489, together with RFC 9989 and RFC 9990. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Failure Reports Are For
sections.content:
A failure report gives detailed information about the failure of a single message, or of a group of similar messages failing for the same reason. The RFC names two purposes. One is to help a Domain Owner find the cause of failures seen in aggregate reports (RFC 9990). The other is to let the owner quickly spot harmful messages that abuse its domain directly.

The cost is that a report can contain header fields or even the entire message, which may include personally identifiable information (PII). Owners should weigh that when deciding whether to ask for reports, and receivers when deciding what to include or redact, or whether to create reports at all.
sections.eli5: A tally says how many bad letters arrived. A failure report is a copy of one bad letter, so the school can see what went wrong. That copy might include private details.

sections.title: When and How Reports Are Sent
sections.content:
Failure reports are normally generated almost immediately after the Mail Receiver detects a DMARC failure, rather than waiting for an aggregate report. They carry more than an aggregate report does, which helps the consumer decide whether the failing message was one the owner meant to authenticate or one that used the domain without authorization. They should include as much of the headers and body as possible, within the reporting party's privacy policies.

The destinations and timing come from the ruf and fo tags of the DMARC Policy Record, defined in RFC 9989. With several URIs, the generator MUST try to deliver to each of them, and external destinations MUST be verified. Generators MUST NOT consider ruf tags in records with psd=y unless the parties have a specific agreement. They also MUST rate-limit outgoing reports.

This document covers only DMARC failure reports. DKIM and SPF failure reports remain in RFC 6591. A receiver MAY send those instead of, or in addition to, the DMARC type, depending on its own policy, the failure and the fo tag.
sections.eli5: As soon as the post office spots a fake letter, it sends the school a note about that one letter, but it must not flood the school with notes.

sections.title: The Reporting Format Update
sections.content:
Reports use the Abuse Reporting Format from RFC 6591, and this document updates it. A DMARC failure report includes these header fields:

  • Identity-Alignment: REQUIRED, defined by this document.
  • Delivery-Result: OPTIONAL.
  • DKIM-Domain, DKIM-Identity, DKIM-Selector: REQUIRED for DKIM failures of an aligned identifier.
  • DKIM-Canonicalized-Header, DKIM-Canonicalized-Body: OPTIONAL when reporting a DKIM failure.
  • SPF-DNS: REQUIRED for an SPF failure of an aligned identifier.

Identity-Alignment holds a comma-separated list of the mechanisms (dkim, spf, each at most once) that failed to authenticate an aligned identity, or the keyword none if all attempted methods succeeded. The Auth-Failure type dmarc is added for reports generated because some or all mechanisms failed to produce aligned identifiers. A generator MAY also independently produce an ARF message for any underlying method.
sections.eli5: The note has a special box that lists which of the two checks, the stamp check or the signature check, failed, or says none if both were fine.

sections.title: External Destinations and Transport
sections.content:
Failure reports may be sent outside the Organizational Domain that asked for them, for example to a contracted processing service. The receiver MUST use the verification procedure in Section 4 of RFC 9990, using the ruf tag where that procedure says rua. That stops an attacker from pointing reports at a victim and then sending mail built to trigger them. It also stops a domain owner from forcing unwanted messages and privacy issues on an outside party.

Email streams carrying failure reports SHOULD be DMARC-aligned. Reporters are recommended to rate-limit reports to any recipient. Unaligned reports may in turn produce further failure reports, which could cause mail loops.
sections.eli5: Before sending notes to someone else's address, the post office checks that the person really agreed to get them. Notes should also carry the school's own seal, so they do not start an endless back-and-forth.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls the privacy concerns significant. Reports can expose PII and non-public information from failing messages, including sender and recipient identifiers and, potentially, the whole message. Examples given are product launches, employee termination notices and calendar data. Even broken calendar invitations can leak private communications. A report can also reveal final destinations, such as members of a mailing list, or forwarding targets the owner did not know about.

Because of this, the RFC notes that many large providers limit or entirely disable failure reports and rely on aggregate reports instead. Operators that enable them are strongly encouraged to limit scope and duration to targeted diagnostics, control and validate reporting URIs, redact message bodies and header fields, and always use secure channels.

Unredacted reports can also spread spam, phishing or malware. Generators can substitute hxxp for http and remove attachments. Consumers can isolate report streams, use sandboxes and network segmentation, and limit access to trained people. Redaction follows RFC 6590.
sections.eli5: Copying a whole letter can show private things like secret plans. So the post office should black out the private parts or skip copying at all, and the school should keep the copies somewhere safe.

sections.title: Denial of Service
sections.content:
Failure reports can be turned into an attack. Someone sends many messages that appear to come from the victim Domain Owner and fail both SPF and DKIM, so participating receivers send large numbers of reports to the owner or its delegates.

Receivers are therefore encouraged to aggregate reports as much as practical, using the Incidents field of the abuse report format (RFC 5965). The aim is to report different failure conditions, not every single failure. Suggested pruning techniques are to store reports for a while so that like incidents can be consolidated, and to apply rate limits, such as a maximum number of reports per minute with the rest discarded.
sections.eli5: If a prankster sends a million fake letters, the school should not get a million notes. The post office bundles similar ones into one note.
